lessons.title: Angles and Angle Measurement
lessons.description: Understand degrees, radians, and how to convert between them.
lessons.formula:
Degrees to Radians: radians = degrees × π/180
Radians to Degrees: degrees = radians × 180/π
Full circle = 360° = 2π radians
Right angle = 90° = π/2
Straight angle = 180° = π
lessons.content:
Angle measurement is one of the oldest concepts in mathematics, dating back to ancient Babylonian astronomers who first divided the circle into 360 equal parts. This division was likely chosen because 360 is approximately the number of days in a year and is highly divisible, making calculations convenient. The Babylonian system of degrees remains the most commonly used angular measurement in everyday life, navigation, and many practical applications.

In advanced mathematics and science, however, the radian is the preferred unit. A radian is defined by the arc length subtended on a unit circle: one radian is the angle that creates an arc equal in length to the radius of the circle. Since the circumference of a unit circle is 2π, a full rotation equals 2π radians. The radian is a dimensionless unit that simplifies many formulas in calculus and physics, making trigonometric derivatives and integrals much cleaner than they would be in degrees.

Converting between degrees and radians is straightforward using proportional reasoning. Since 360° = 2π radians, you multiply degrees by π/180 to get radians, or multiply radians by 180/π to get degrees. Coterminal angles share the same terminal side and can be found by adding or subtracting multiples of 360° (or 2π radians). Mastering these conversions and understanding standard position (vertex at origin, initial side on positive x-axis) are essential foundations for all of trigonometry.
steps: Identify the angle you need to convert and its unit (degrees or radians).
To convert degrees to radians, multiply the angle by π/180.
To convert radians to degrees, multiply the angle by 180/π.
Simplify the resulting fraction by canceling common factors with π.
To find coterminal angles, add or subtract 360° (or 2π radians) as many times as needed.

examples.title: Convert 45° to Radians
examples.text: Multiply 45° by π/180: 45×π/180 = π/4. So 45° = π/4 radians. This is one of the most commonly used radian values in trigonometry.

lessons.tip: Memorize the common angle conversions: 0°=0, 30°=π/6, 45°=π/4, 60°=π/3, 90°=π/2, 180°=π, 270°=3π/2, 360°=2π. Knowing these by heart saves enormous time on exams and in applications.

quiz.q: Convert 60° to radians.
What is 3π/2 radians in degrees?
Which of the following is a coterminal angle with 45°?
quiz.explanation: Adding 360° gives a coterminal angle: 45° + 360° = 405°, which shares the same terminal side as 45°.

quiz.q: A full circle is equal to how many radians?
quiz.explanation: A full circle = 360° = 2π radians. This is because the circumference of a unit circle is 2π.

lessons.title: SOH-CAH-TOA: Right Triangle Trigonometric Ratios
lessons.description: Master the three primary trig ratios: sine, cosine, and tangent.
lessons.formula:
SOH: sin(θ) = Opposite / Hypotenuse
CAH: cos(θ) = Adjacent / Hypotenuse
TOA: tan(θ) = Opposite / Adjacent
Also: tan(θ) = sin(θ) / cos(θ)
lessons.content:
SOH-CAH-TOA is the foundational mnemonic for remembering the three primary trigonometric ratios in a right triangle. Each letter represents a key relationship: Sine = Opposite over Hypotenuse, Cosine = Adjacent over Hypotenuse, and Tangent = Opposite over Adjacent. Before applying any ratio, you must correctly identify which side is the opposite (across from the angle), the adjacent (next to the angle but not the hypotenuse), and the hypotenuse (always the longest side, opposite the right angle).

To label a right triangle for trigonometry, first locate the reference angle θ. The side directly across from θ is the opposite side. The side that forms one leg of angle θ (but is not the hypotenuse) is the adjacent side. The hypotenuse is always across from the 90° angle and never changes regardless of which acute angle is your reference. Labeling correctly is half the battle—once labeled, simply substitute the side lengths into the appropriate ratio.

When solving for a missing side, set up the equation using the appropriate trig ratio, then use algebra to isolate the unknown. For example, if you know the hypotenuse and the angle, use cosine to find the adjacent side. If you know two sides and need the angle, use the inverse trigonometric function (sin⁻¹, cos⁻¹, or tan⁻¹). The relationship tan = sin/cos is also important: it means tangent is undefined wherever cosine equals zero (at 90° and 270°).
steps: Identify the right angle and the reference angle θ in the triangle.
Label the three sides: opposite (across from θ), adjacent (next to θ), and hypotenuse (longest side, across from 90°).
Choose the correct trig ratio: use SOH for opposite/hypotenuse, CAH for adjacent/hypotenuse, or TOA for opposite/adjacent.
Substitute the known values into the ratio and set up the equation.
Solve the equation using algebra (or inverse trig functions) to find the missing value.

examples.title: Find sin, cos, and tan for a 3-4-5 Triangle
examples.text: For a right triangle with opposite=3, adjacent=4, hypotenuse=5: sin(θ) = 3/5 = 0.6, cos(θ) = 4/5 = 0.8, tan(θ) = 3/4 = 0.75. Verify: tan = sin/cos = 0.6/0.8 = 0.75 ✓.

examples.title: Finding a Missing Side
examples.text: In a right triangle, if the hypotenuse = 10 and angle θ = 30°, find the opposite side. Using sin(30°) = opposite/10, we get opposite = 10 × sin(30°) = 10 × 0.5 = 5.

lessons.tip: Always label your triangle BEFORE choosing a ratio. A common mistake is confusing opposite and adjacent. Remember: opposite is always across from the angle, and adjacent is the 'other leg' (not the hypotenuse).

quiz.q: In a right triangle with opposite=6 and hypotenuse=10, what is sin(θ)?
quiz.explanation: sin(θ) = opposite/hypotenuse = 6/10 = 3/5.

quiz.q: Which trig ratio uses opposite over adjacent?
quiz.explanation: TOA: Tangent = Opposite / Adjacent.

quiz.q: If cos(θ) = 0.8 and the hypotenuse is 15, what is the adjacent side?
quiz.explanation: cos(θ) = adjacent/hypotenuse, so 0.8 = adjacent/15, giving adjacent = 15 × 0.8 = 12.

quiz.q: tan(θ) = sin(θ)/cos(θ). If sin(θ)=0.6 and cos(θ)=0.8, what is tan(θ)?

lessons.title: The Unit Circle
lessons.description: Explore the unit circle and how it defines trigonometric values for all angles.
lessons.formula:
On the unit circle:
cos(θ) = x-coordinate
sin(θ) = y-coordinate
Key angles:
0° = (1, 0)
30° = (√3/2, 1/2)
45° = (√2/2, √2/2)
60° = (1/2, √3/2)
90° = (0, 1)

Reference angles and quadrants determine signs.
lessons.content:
The unit circle is a circle centered at the origin with a radius of exactly 1. It is one of the most powerful tools in trigonometry because it allows us to define sine and cosine for any angle—not just the acute angles in a right triangle. Starting from the positive x-axis, we rotate counterclockwise by angle θ, and the terminal side intersects the circle at a point (x, y). By definition, cos(θ) = x and sin(θ) = y. This elegant connection between angles and coordinates is the bridge between geometry and trigonometry.

The unit circle is divided into four quadrants, and the signs of sine and cosine change depending on the quadrant. In Quadrant I (0° to 90°), both sin and cos are positive. In Quadrant II (90° to 180°), sin is positive but cos is negative. In Quadrant III (180° to 270°), both are negative. In Quadrant IV (270° to 360°), sin is negative and cos is positive. The mnemonic ASTC (All Students Take Calculus) helps: All positive in QI, Sine in QII, Tangent in QIII, Cosine in QIV.

Reference angles are the acute angles formed by the terminal side and the x-axis. Every angle has a reference angle between 0° and 90°. To find the exact trig value of any special angle, determine its reference angle, find the value for that reference angle (using the memorized special values), and then apply the correct sign based on the quadrant. The special angles at 0°, 30°, 45°, 60°, and 90° (and their multiples) have exact values expressed in terms of square roots that every trigonometry student must memorize.
steps: Start at (1, 0) on the positive x-axis and rotate counterclockwise by the given angle θ.
Determine which quadrant the terminal side lands in to know the signs of sin and cos.
Find the reference angle: the acute angle between the terminal side and the x-axis.
Use the memorized special angle values for the reference angle to get the absolute values of sin and cos.
Apply the correct signs based on the quadrant (use ASTC: All, Sine, Tangent, Cosine).

examples.title: Find cos(150°) Using the Unit Circle
examples.text: 150° is in Quadrant II. Reference angle = 180° - 150° = 30°. cos(30°) = √3/2. Since cos is negative in QII, cos(150°) = -√3/2.

examples.title: Find sin(225°) Using the Unit Circle
examples.text: 225° is in Quadrant III. Reference angle = 225° - 180° = 45°. sin(45°) = √2/2. Since sin is negative in QIII, sin(225°) = -√2/2.

lessons.tip: Draw the unit circle and fill in the special angle coordinates yourself at least 10 times. The act of drawing it builds muscle memory. Focus on just the first quadrant first (0° to 90°), then use symmetry and quadrant signs to fill in the rest.

quiz.q: What are the coordinates of the point on the unit circle at 60°?
quiz.explanation: At 60°: cos(60°) = 1/2 (x-coordinate) and sin(60°) = √3/2 (y-coordinate), so the point is (1/2, √3/2).

quiz.q: In which quadrant is sin(θ) positive and cos(θ) negative?
quiz.explanation: In Quadrant II (90° to 180°), sine is positive (y-values are positive) and cosine is negative (x-values are negative).

quiz.q: What is the reference angle for 300°?
quiz.explanation: 300° is in QIV. Reference angle = 360° - 300° = 60°.

quiz.q: What is cos(90°)?
quiz.explanation: At 90°, the point on the unit circle is (0, 1). cos(90°) = x-coordinate = 0.

lessons.title: Radian Measure and Arc Length
lessons.description: Apply radian measure to calculate arc length and sector area.
lessons.formula:
Arc length: s = rθ (θ in radians)
Area of sector: A = ½r²θ (θ in radians)
Circumference = 2πr
When θ = 2π, s = 2πr (full circle)
When θ = π, s = πr (semicircle)
lessons.content:
One of the most elegant features of radian measure is its direct relationship to arc length. On a circle of radius r, if a central angle θ (in radians) subtends an arc, the length of that arc is given by the simple formula s = rθ. This formula only works when θ is in radians—if you use degrees, you need an extra conversion factor, which is precisely why radians are preferred in calculus. The beauty of s = rθ is that the radian was literally defined to make this formula work without any constant.

The formula for the area of a sector (the pie-slice region bounded by two radii and an arc) is equally clean: A = ½r²θ, where θ is in radians. You can verify this by noting that the full circle area is πr², and a full circle corresponds to θ = 2π radians. Plugging in: A = ½ r² (2π) = πr², which matches the known area formula. For a semicircle (θ = π), the area is ½ r² π = πr²/2, which is exactly half the circle area.

These formulas have countless real-world applications. Engineers use arc length to design curved roads and railway tracks. Architects use sector area to calculate the area of curved windows or arched doorways. In physics, angular velocity (measured in radians per second) uses radian measure to describe rotational motion, and the relationship between linear velocity v and angular velocity ω is v = rω, which directly comes from the arc length formula differentiated with respect to time.
steps: Ensure the central angle θ is in radians. If it is in degrees, convert using θ × π/180.
Identify the radius r of the circle.
For arc length: multiply r by θ using the formula s = rθ.
For sector area: square the radius, multiply by θ, and halve the result using A = ½r²θ.
Check your answer: arc length should be less than the full circumference (2πr), and sector area should be less than the full area (πr²).

examples.title: Finding Arc Length
examples.text: A circle has radius 5 cm. Find the arc length subtended by a central angle of π/3 radians. Using s = rθ: s = 5 × π/3 = 5π/3 ≈ 5.24 cm. This makes sense since π/3 = 60°, which is one-sixth of the circle.

examples.title: Finding Sector Area
examples.text: A circle has radius 8 meters. Find the area of a sector with central angle 2 radians. Using A = ½r²θ: A = ½ × 64 × 2 = 64 square meters. Since 2 radians is about 114.6°, this is roughly one-third of the full area (64π ≈ 201), which checks out.

lessons.tip: The arc length formula s = rθ ONLY works with radians. If your angle is in degrees, convert first! A quick check: if s = rθ gives a value larger than 2πr (the full circumference), something is wrong.

quiz.q: A circle has radius 6 and central angle π/4 radians. What is the arc length?
A sector has radius 10 and central angle π/2. What is its area?
The formula s = rθ requires the angle to be measured in:
quiz.explanation: The arc length formula s = rθ only works when θ is measured in radians.

quiz.q: What is the arc length of a full circle with radius r?
quiz.explanation: A full circle has θ = 2π radians, so s = r(2π) = 2πr, which is the circumference.

lessons.title: Graphing Sine and Cosine Functions
lessons.description: Graph y = sin(x) and y = cos(x) with amplitude, period, and transformations.
lessons.formula:
y = A·sin(B(x - C)) + D
y = A·cos(B(x - C)) + D

Amplitude = |A|
Period = 2π/|B|
Phase shift = C
Vertical shift = D
Midline: y = D
lessons.content:
The graphs of y = sin(x) and y = cos(x) are smooth, repeating curves called sinusoidal waves. Both have a period of 2π (they complete one full cycle over an interval of 2π) and an amplitude of 1 (they oscillate between -1 and 1). The key difference is the starting point: sin(x) begins at 0 and rises to its maximum, while cos(x) begins at its maximum of 1 and descends. The midline of both basic graphs is y = 0 (the x-axis).

Transformations of these basic graphs follow a predictable pattern described by the general form y = A·sin(B(x - C)) + D. The amplitude |A| stretches or compresses the graph vertically—a larger |A| means taller waves. The factor B affects the period: period = 2π/|B|, so larger B values produce more frequent oscillations. The phase shift C moves the graph horizontally (note the minus sign: if C is positive, the graph shifts right). The vertical shift D moves the entire graph up or down, establishing the midline at y = D.

To graph a transformed sine or cosine function, start by identifying the five key features: amplitude, period, phase shift, vertical shift, and midline. Then plot five critical points over one complete cycle: the starting point, maximum, midline crossing, minimum, and ending midline crossing. For y = sin(x), these occur at x = 0, π/2, π, 3π/2, 2π respectively. Connect them with a smooth wave and repeat the pattern. Always use exact values at special angles for precision.
steps: Identify A (amplitude), B (frequency), C (phase shift), and D (vertical shift) from the equation y = A·sin(B(x-C))+D.
Calculate the period: Period = 2π/|B|. Determine the interval for one complete cycle.
Find the starting x-value by applying the phase shift: start at x = C.
Mark the five key points across one period: start, max, midline, min, and end.
Plot the points and connect with a smooth sinusoidal curve, then repeat the pattern for additional cycles.

examples.title: Graph y = 2sin(x)
examples.text: Amplitude = |2| = 2 (wave goes from -2 to 2). Period = 2π/1 = 2π (normal period). No phase or vertical shift. The graph looks like a normal sine wave stretched vertically by a factor of 2, oscillating between y = -2 and y = 2.

examples.title: Graph y = 3cos(2x - π) + 1
examples.text: Rewrite as y = 3cos(2(x - π/2)) + 1. Amplitude = 3, Period = 2π/2 = π, Phase shift = π/2 (right), Vertical shift = 1 (midline y = 1). The wave oscillates between y = -2 and y = 4, completing one cycle from x = π/2 to x = 3π/2.

lessons.tip: Always rewrite the equation in the form y = A·sin(B(x - C)) + D by factoring out B from the x-term before identifying the phase shift. A common error is to misread the phase shift from an unfactored form like y = sin(2x - π).

quiz.q: What is the amplitude of y = 4sin(x)?
quiz.explanation: Amplitude = |A| = |4| = 4.

quiz.q: What is the period of y = cos(3x)?
quiz.explanation: Period = 2π/|B| = 2π/3.

quiz.q: The midline of y = sin(x) + 3 is:
quiz.explanation: The vertical shift D = 3, so the midline is y = 3.

quiz.q: What is the phase shift of y = sin(x - π/4)?
quiz.explanation: Phase shift = C = π/4, and since the form is (x - C), the graph shifts π/4 units to the right.

lessons.title: Graphing Tangent and Other Trig Functions
lessons.description: Graph y = tan(x), cot(x), sec(x), and csc(x) including asymptotes.
lessons.formula:
tan(x) = sin(x)/cos(x)
cot(x) = cos(x)/sin(x)
sec(x) = 1/cos(x)
csc(x) = 1/sin(x)

Period of tan & cot = π
Period of sec & csc = 2π
tan asymptotes: x = π/2 + nπ (where cos(x)=0)
cot asymptotes: x = nπ (where sin(x)=0)
lessons.content:
While sine and cosine produce smooth, bounded waves, the tangent function has a dramatically different shape. Since tan(x) = sin(x)/cos(x), it is undefined wherever cos(x) = 0, creating vertical asymptotes at x = π/2 + nπ (every 90°). Between consecutive asymptotes, the tangent function increases smoothly from negative infinity to positive infinity, crossing the x-axis at multiples of π. This repeating pattern has a period of π (half the period of sine and cosine), meaning the graph repeats every 180° instead of every 360°.

The cotangent function cot(x) = cos(x)/sin(x) is the reciprocal of tangent. It is undefined where sin(x) = 0 (at x = nπ), giving asymptotes at the multiples of π. Between its asymptotes, cotangent decreases from positive infinity to negative infinity. The secant function sec(x) = 1/cos(x) has the same asymptotes as tangent (where cos = 0) and a period of 2π. Its graph consists of U-shaped curves that open upward above y = 1 and downward below y = -1, with the cos(x) wave as its midline.

The cosecant function csc(x) = 1/sin(x) is undefined where sin(x) = 0 (at x = nπ), and its period is 2π. Its graph uses the sine wave as a reference. When sin(x) approaches 0, csc(x) shoots toward ±∞, creating asymptotes. When sin(x) = 1 (at π/2), csc(x) = 1, and when sin(x) = -1 (at 3π/2), csc(x) = -1. A powerful strategy for graphing these functions is to first sketch the corresponding sine, cosine, or tangent graph, then use the reciprocal relationship to draw the transformed curve.
steps: Identify the function and its basic form (tan, cot, sec, or csc).
Determine the asymptotes: where the denominator of the reciprocal relationship equals zero.
Mark the period: π for tan/cot, 2π for sec/csc.
Find key points between asymptotes: x-intercepts (for tan/cot) or min/max points (for sec/csc).
Plot the points and draw the characteristic curves, approaching but never touching the asymptotes.

examples.title: Graph y = tan(x)
examples.text: Asymptotes at x = π/2 + nπ. Period = π. Between asymptotes at x = -π/2 and π/2, the curve passes through (0, 0) and rises from -∞ to +∞. The pattern repeats every π units.

examples.title: Graph y = sec(x)
examples.text: Asymptotes at x = π/2 + nπ (same as tan). Period = 2π. Minimum value y = 1 at x = 0, y = -1 at x = π. The graph consists of U-shaped branches opening upward from the local minima and downward from the local maxima, never crossing between y = -1 and y = 1.

lessons.tip: To graph sec(x) or csc(x), first sketch cos(x) or sin(x) lightly as a guide. Then draw the reciprocal curve: where the guide curve is near 0, draw the asymptote; where the guide curve peaks at 1 or -1, draw the reciprocal touching the same value.

quiz.q: Where does tan(x) have vertical asymptotes?
quiz.explanation: tan(x) = sin(x)/cos(x) is undefined where cos(x) = 0, which occurs at x = π/2 + nπ.

quiz.q: What is the period of cot(x)?
quiz.explanation: The period of both tan(x) and cot(x) is π.

quiz.q: sec(x) is the reciprocal of which function?
quiz.explanation: sec(x) = 1/cos(x). Secant is the reciprocal of cosine.

quiz.q: What is the period of csc(x)?
quiz.explanation: csc(x) = 1/sin(x) shares the same period as sin(x), which is 2π.

lessons.title: Fundamental Trigonometric Identities
lessons.description: Master Pythagorean identities, reciprocal identities, and quotient identities.
lessons.formula:
Pythagorean Identities:
sin²θ + cos²θ = 1
tan²θ + 1 = sec²θ
1 + cot²θ = csc²θ

Reciprocal Identities:
csc(θ) = 1/sin(θ)
sec(θ) = 1/cos(θ)
cot(θ) = 1/tan(θ)

Quotient Identities:
tan(θ) = sin(θ)/cos(θ)
cot(θ) = cos(θ)/sin(θ)
lessons.content:
Trigonometric identities are equations that are true for all values of the variable where both sides are defined. Unlike equations you solve for x, identities are always true—they express fundamental relationships between trigonometric functions. The three categories of fundamental identities are Pythagorean identities, reciprocal identities, and quotient identities. Together, they form the toolkit for simplifying expressions, verifying other identities, and solving equations.

The most important identity is sin²θ + cos²θ = 1, which follows directly from the Pythagorean theorem applied to the unit circle: if a point (x, y) lies on the unit circle, then x² + y² = 1, and since x = cos(θ) and y = sin(θ), the result follows. Dividing this identity by cos²θ gives tan²θ + 1 = sec²θ, and dividing by sin²θ gives 1 + cot²θ = csc²θ. These three Pythagorean identities are used constantly in simplification.

The reciprocal identities simply define the less common trig functions: csc = 1/sin, sec = 1/cos, and cot = 1/tan. The quotient identities define tangent and cotangent as ratios: tan = sin/cos and cot = cos/sin. When verifying a complex identity, a common strategy is to work on one side only (usually the more complicated side), substituting identities to simplify until it matches the other side. Another approach is to convert everything to sine and cosine using quotient and reciprocal identities, then simplify using the Pythagorean identity.
steps: Identify which identity type(s) you need: Pythagorean, reciprocal, or quotient.
If simplifying, start with the more complex side of the equation.
Replace tan, cot, sec, and csc with sine and cosine using quotient and reciprocal identities.
Apply the Pythagorean identity sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 to simplify (or its variants).
Continue simplifying using algebra (factoring, combining fractions) until both sides match.

examples.title: Verify: tanθ · cosθ = sinθ
examples.text: Start with the left side: tanθ · cosθ = (sinθ/cosθ) · cosθ = sinθ · (cosθ/cosθ) = sinθ · 1 = sinθ. The left side equals the right side, so the identity is verified.

examples.title: Simplify: sec²θ - tan²θ
examples.text: Using the identity tan²θ + 1 = sec²θ, rearrange to get sec²θ - tan²θ = 1. So the expression simplifies to exactly 1 for all values where defined.

lessons.tip: When verifying identities, work on ONE side only. Never move terms across the equals sign (that is solving, not verifying). Converting everything to sine and cosine first almost always works as a fallback strategy.

quiz.q: Which identity is sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 classified as?
quiz.explanation: sin²θ + cos²θ = 1 is a Pythagorean identity, derived from the Pythagorean theorem.

quiz.q: What is 1 + tan²θ equal to?
quiz.explanation: The Pythagorean identity states: tan²θ + 1 = sec²θ.

quiz.q: csc(θ) is equal to:
quiz.explanation: csc(θ) = 1/sin(θ) by the reciprocal identity.

quiz.q: Simplify: sinθ/cosθ
quiz.explanation: By the quotient identity, tan(θ) = sin(θ)/cos(θ).

lessons.title: Solving Trigonometric Equations
lessons.description: Solve equations like 2sin(x) = 1 and cos²(x) - cos(x) = 0 for all solutions.
lessons.formula:
Steps to solve trig equations:
1. Isolate the trig function
2. Use inverse trig to find the reference angle
3. Apply quadrant rules for all solutions in [0, 2π)
4. Add 2πn for the general solution

For sin(x) = a: x = θ + 2πn or x = π - θ + 2πn
For cos(x) = a: x = θ + 2πn or x = -θ + 2πn
For tan(x) = a: x = θ + πn
lessons.content:
Solving trigonometric equations combines algebraic techniques with your knowledge of the unit circle. The goal is to find all angle values (usually in radians) that satisfy the equation. Unlike linear equations that typically have one solution, trigonometric equations often have infinitely many solutions because trigonometric functions are periodic. The general solution expresses all answers compactly using the notation “+ 2πn” (where n is any integer) to capture every repetition.

The first step is always to isolate the trigonometric function using algebra. For example, in 2sin(x) = 1, divide both sides by 2 to get sin(x) = 1/2. Then use the inverse trigonometric function (sin⁻¹) to find the reference angle: x = sin⁻¹(1/2) = π/6. But this is only one solution! Since sin is positive in Quadrants I and II, the other solution in [0, 2π) is x = π - π/6 = 5π/6. The general solution is x = π/6 + 2πn and x = 5π/6 + 2πn.

For more complex equations like cos²(x) - cos(x) = 0, use factoring: cos(x)[cos(x) - 1] = 0, giving cos(x) = 0 or cos(x) = 1. Solve each separately. When squaring both sides or applying identities during the solving process, always check for extraneous solutions—answers that satisfy the manipulated equation but not the original. The unit circle remains your best tool for finding the correct quadrant solutions.
steps: Use algebra to isolate the trigonometric function on one side of the equation.
If necessary, use identities (Pythagorean, factoring) to reduce to a single trig function.
Apply the inverse trigonometric function to find the reference angle θ.
Use the unit circle and quadrant signs to find all solutions within one period [0, 2π).
Write the general solution by adding 2πn (or πn for tangent) to each base solution, where n is any integer.

examples.title: Solve 2sin(x) = 1 for all solutions
examples.text: Isolate: sin(x) = 1/2. Reference angle = sin⁻¹(1/2) = π/6. sin is positive in QI and QII, so solutions in [0, 2π) are x = π/6 and x = 5π/6. General solution: x = π/6 + 2πn or x = 5π/6 + 2πn.

examples.title: Solve cos²(x) - cos(x) = 0
examples.text: Factor: cos(x)[cos(x) - 1] = 0. Case 1: cos(x) = 0 → x = π/2, 3π/2. Case 2: cos(x) = 1 → x = 0. General solution: x = π/2 + πn, or x = 0 + 2πn.

lessons.tip: Always find ALL solutions within [0, 2π) before writing the general solution. Missing a quadrant solution is the most common error. Draw the unit circle and physically point to where the solutions are.

quiz.q: Solve sin(x) = √2/2 for all solutions in [0, 2π).
quiz.explanation: sin(x) = √2/2. Reference angle = π/4. sin is positive in QI and QII, so x = π/4 and x = π - π/4 = 3π/4.

quiz.q: What is the general solution for tan(x) = 1?
quiz.explanation: tan(x) = 1 gives x = π/4. Since tan has period π, the general solution is x = π/4 + πn.

quiz.q: How many solutions does cos(x) = -1 have in [0, 2π)?
quiz.explanation: cos(x) = -1 only at x = π in the interval [0, 2π). Just one solution.

quiz.q: When solving trig equations, what does + 2πn represent?
quiz.explanation: Adding 2πn (where n is any integer) captures all periodic repetitions of the solutions.

lessons.title: Sum and Difference Formulas
lessons.description: Use sum and difference identities to find exact values and simplify expressions.
lessons.formula:
Sum and Difference Formulas:

sin(A + B) = sinA·cosB + cosA·sinB
sin(A - B) = sinA·cosB - cosA·sinB

cos(A + B) = cosA·cosB - sinA·sinB
cos(A - B) = cosA·cosB + sinA·sinB

tan(A + B) = (tanA + tanB)/(1 - tanA·tanB)
tan(A - B) = (tanA - tanB)/(1 + tanA·tanB)
lessons.content:
The sum and difference formulas allow you to find exact trigonometric values for angles that are not on the unit circle by breaking them into combinations of known angles. For example, sin(75°) is not a standard unit circle value, but since 75° = 45° + 30°, we can use the sum formula to compute it exactly. These formulas are derived from the geometry of the unit circle and are among the most practically useful identities in trigonometry.

The key pattern to memorize is the sign convention: for sine, the signs in the sum and difference formulas match (+ for A+B, - for A-B). For cosine, the signs are reversed (- for A+B, + for A-B). This is often remembered with the phrase “sine keeps its sign, cosine swaps its sign.” The tangent formulas follow the same sign pattern as sine. Understanding these patterns prevents sign errors, which are the most common mistake when applying these formulas.

These formulas also give rise to the cofunction identities: sin(90° - θ) = cos(θ) and cos(90° - θ) = sin(θ). This is because sin(π/2 - θ) = sin(π/2)cos(θ) - cos(π/2)sin(θ) = 1·cos(θ) - 0·sin(θ) = cos(θ). The sum and difference formulas are also essential in calculus for proving derivative rules and in physics for analyzing wave interference and superposition.
steps: Identify the angle as a sum or difference of two known angles (from the unit circle special angles).
Select the correct formula (sin, cos, or tan) and apply the sum or difference version as needed.
Substitute the exact values of sin and cos for each of the known angles.
Simplify the expression by performing the arithmetic (multiply, add, or subtract).
Rationalize the denominator if needed and simplify radicals to get the final exact value.

examples.title: Find the Exact Value of sin(75°)
Find cos(15°) Using a Difference Formula

lessons.tip: Memorize the sign pattern: Sine keeps its sign (same sign in the formula as in the angle operation). Cosine swaps its sign (opposite sign in the formula). This trick saves you from constantly looking up the formulas.

quiz.q: sin(A + B) equals:
quiz.explanation: sin(A + B) = sinA·cosB + cosA·sinB.

quiz.q: cos(A - B) equals:
quiz.explanation: cos(A - B) = cosA·cosB + sinA·sinB (note: the minus in the angle becomes plus in the formula).

quiz.q: To find sin(105°), which angle split would you use?
quiz.explanation: 105° = 60° + 45°, and both 60° and 45° have known exact values on the unit circle.

quiz.q: sin(90° - θ) simplifies to:
quiz.explanation: This is the cofunction identity: sin(90° - θ) = cos(θ).

lessons.title: Double and Half Angle Formulas
lessons.description: Use double angle and half angle identities for simplification and exact values.
lessons.formula:
Double Angle Formulas:
sin(2θ) = 2sin(θ)cos(θ)
cos(2θ) = cos²(θ) - sin²(θ)
         = 2cos²(θ) - 1
         = 1 - 2sin²(θ)

Half Angle Formulas:
sin(θ/2) = ±√((1 - cos(θ))/2)
cos(θ/2) = ±√((1 + cos(θ))/2)

Power Reduction:
sin²(θ) = (1 - cos(2θ))/2
cos²(θ) = (1 + cos(2θ))/2
lessons.content:
Double angle formulas express trigonometric functions of 2θ in terms of functions of θ. The sine double angle formula is straightforward: sin(2θ) = 2sin(θ)cos(θ). The cosine double angle formula has three equivalent forms, which is incredibly useful because you can choose whichever version best fits the given information. If you know both sin and cos, use cos² - sin². If you only know cos, use 2cos² - 1. If you only know sin, use 1 - 2sin².

The half angle formulas go in the opposite direction, expressing functions of θ/2 in terms of functions of θ. The ± sign in front of the square root is determined by the quadrant in which θ/2 lies. For example, if θ = 240°, then θ/2 = 120°, which is in Quadrant II where sin is positive and cos is negative. So sin(120°) = +√((1 - cos(240°))/2) but cos(120°) = -√((1 + cos(240°))/2).

Power reduction formulas (also called power-reducing identities) allow you to rewrite squared trig functions in terms of cos(2θ), effectively “reducing the power” from 2 to 1. These are essential in calculus for integrating powers of sine and cosine, and in electrical engineering for analyzing AC circuits using RMS values. The formulas sin²θ = (1 - cos(2θ))/2 and cos²θ = (1 + cos(2θ))/2 are among the most frequently used identities in applied mathematics.
steps: Identify whether you need a double angle formula (finding trig of 2θ) or half angle formula (finding trig of θ/2).
For double angle: substitute into the appropriate formula. Choose the cosine form that matches your known values.
For half angle: compute (1 ± cos(θ))/2 under the square root.
Determine the sign of the ± by identifying which quadrant the resulting angle is in.
Simplify the square root expression to get the exact value.

examples.title: Find cos(2θ) if sin(θ) = 3/5
examples.text: Using cos(2θ) = 1 - 2sin²(θ): cos(2θ) = 1 - 2(9/25) = 1 - 18/25 = 7/25. We chose the form with sin² since only sin was given.

examples.title: Find sin(15°) Using a Half Angle Formula

lessons.tip: For the ± sign in half angle formulas: determine the quadrant of θ/2, not θ. If θ = 300°, then θ/2 = 150° (QII), where sin is positive and cos is negative. Always check the quadrant of the half angle.

quiz.q: sin(2θ) = 2sin(θ)cos(θ). If sin(θ) = 0.6 and cos(θ) = 0.8, what is sin(2θ)?
Which is NOT a form of cos(2θ)?
quiz.explanation: 2sin(θ)cos(θ) is sin(2θ), not cos(2θ).

quiz.q: sin²(θ) can be rewritten as:
quiz.explanation: The power reduction formula: sin²(θ) = (1 - cos(2θ))/2.

quiz.q: In the half angle formula for sin(θ/2), the ± sign depends on:
options: Whether θ is positive or negative
quiz.explanation: The ± sign is determined by the quadrant in which the half angle θ/2 lies, based on whether the function is positive or negative in that quadrant.

lessons.title: Law of Sines
lessons.description: Use the Law of Sines to solve any triangle when you know an angle and its opposite side.
lessons.formula:
Law of Sines:
a/sin(A) = b/sin(B) = c/sin(C)

Applicable for: AAS, ASA, SSA
NOT applicable for: SSS, SAS (use Law of Cosines)

Ambiguous Case (SSA):
May have 0, 1, or 2 solutions

Area = ½ab·sin(C)
lessons.content:
The Law of Sines extends trigonometry beyond right triangles to any oblique triangle (a triangle without a right angle). It states that the ratio of each side length to the sine of its opposite angle is constant: a/sin(A) = b/sin(B) = c/sin(C). This elegant relationship allows you to find unknown sides and angles when you have certain combinations of known information, specifically the cases AAS (two angles and a side), ASA (a side and two angles), and SSA (two sides and an angle opposite one of them).

The ambiguous case (SSA) is famously tricky because it can produce zero, one, or two valid triangles. Given sides a and b and angle A opposite side a, compare a to b·sin(A). If a < b·sin(A), no triangle exists (side a is too short to reach the base). If a = b·sin(A), exactly one right triangle forms. If b·sin(A) < a < b, two different triangles are possible (the side can “swing” to two positions). If a ≥ b, exactly one triangle forms. Visualizing this with the side swinging like a pendulum makes the ambiguity intuitive.

The Law of Sines also provides a convenient area formula: Area = ½ab·sin(C), where a and b are two sides and C is the included angle. This is derived from the standard area formula ½ × base × height, where height = b·sin(C). This area formula is especially useful because it works for any triangle and only requires two sides and their included angle—information you often have in navigation and surveying problems.
steps: Verify the triangle type: you need at least one side-angle pair (a known side opposite a known angle).
Set up the Law of Sines proportion: known side/sin(known angle) = unknown side/sin(unknown angle).
Cross-multiply and solve for the unknown value.
For SSA case, check the ambiguous case: determine if 0, 1, or 2 triangles are possible.
Once you have two angles, find the third angle using the fact that all angles sum to 180°.

examples.title: Find a Missing Side Using Law of Sines
examples.text: In triangle ABC, angle A = 40°, angle B = 60°, and side a = 12. Find side b. Using a/sin(A) = b/sin(B): 12/sin(40°) = b/sin(60°). So b = 12·sin(60°)/sin(40°) = 12(0.866)/(0.643) ≈ 16.16.

examples.title: Ambiguous Case: Two Triangles
examples.text: Given angle A = 30°, side a = 8, side b = 16. Since a = 8 < b = 16 and a > b·sin(30°) = 8, there are two possible triangles. Angle B could be sin⁻¹(16·sin(30°)/8) = sin⁻¹(1) = 90°, giving B = 90° or B = 180° - 90° = 90°. Here both solutions yield the same triangle, but if a were slightly different, two distinct triangles would result.

lessons.tip: For the ambiguous case (SSA), always draw the triangle! Visualize side a as a pendulum swinging from the top of side b. The number of times the pendulum reaches the base line tells you the number of solutions: 0, 1, or 2.

quiz.q: The Law of Sines states that a/sin(A) = b/sin(B) = c/sin(C). This can solve which case?
quiz.explanation: The Law of Sines works when you have a side-angle pair: AAS, ASA, and SSA cases.

quiz.q: In the ambiguous case (SSA), when can two triangles exist?
quiz.explanation: Two triangles exist when side a is between b·sin(A) and b in length.

quiz.q: The area of a triangle with sides a=10, b=8, and included angle C=30° is:
If you know all three sides of a triangle (SSS), which law should you use?
quiz.explanation: For SSS (and SAS), use the Law of Cosines. The Law of Sines requires at least one known angle-side pair.

lessons.title: Law of Cosines
lessons.description: Use the Law of Cosines to solve triangles when you know three sides (SSS) or two sides and the included angle (SAS).
lessons.formula:
Law of Cosines:
c² = a² + b² - 2ab·cos(C)
Also: a² = b² + c² - 2bc·cos(A)
      b² = a² + c² - 2ac·cos(B)

Solving for angle:
cos(C) = (a² + b² - c²)/(2ab)

Heron's Formula (area):
s = (a + b + c)/2 (semiperimeter)
Area = √(s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c))
lessons.content:
The Law of Cosines is the generalization of the Pythagorean theorem for all triangles. While the Pythagorean theorem (c² = a² + b²) only works for right triangles, the Law of Cosines adds a correction term: c² = a² + b² - 2ab·cos(C). Notice that when C = 90°, cos(90°) = 0, and the formula reduces to the Pythagorean theorem. The correction term -2ab·cos(C) accounts for how much the triangle deviates from being a right triangle.

The Law of Cosines is essential for two cases that the Law of Sines cannot handle: SSS (three known sides) and SAS (two known sides and their included angle). For SSS, use the rearranged form cos(C) = (a² + b² - c²)/(2ab) to find an angle, then use the Law of Sines or repeat the Law of Cosines for other angles. For SAS, directly compute the unknown side using c² = a² + b² - 2ab·cos(C), then find remaining angles using the Law of Sines or the angle sum.

Heron’s formula is a powerful alternative for finding area when you only know three sides. First compute the semiperimeter s = (a + b + c)/2, then Area = √(s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)). This formula is derived from the Law of Cosines and is especially useful in surveying, construction, and any application where you can measure three sides but not angles. Heron’s formula has been known for over 2,000 years and remains one of the most elegant results in geometry.
steps: Identify the case: SSS (three sides known) or SAS (two sides and included angle known).
For SAS: directly apply c² = a² + b² - 2ab·cos(C) to find the unknown side.
For SSS: use cos(C) = (a² + b² - c²)/(2ab) to find an angle, then take cos⁻¹.
Find remaining angles using the Law of Sines, Law of Cosines, or the angle sum (180° total).
For area with three sides: compute the semiperimeter s, then apply Heron’s formula.

examples.title: Find the Third Side (SAS Case)
examples.text: Triangle has sides a = 7, b = 10, and included angle C = 45°. Using c² = a² + b² - 2ab·cos(C): c² = 49 + 100 - 2(7)(10)cos(45°) = 149 - 140(√2/2) = 149 - 70√2 ≈ 149 - 98.99 = 50.01. So c ≈ 7.07.

lessons.tip: When choosing between Law of Sines and Law of Cosines, ask: do I have a side-angle pair? If yes, use Law of Sines. If no (SSS or SAS), use Law of Cosines. For SSS, always find the largest angle first using the Law of Cosines, then use Law of Sines for the rest.

quiz.q: The Law of Cosines for side c is:
quiz.explanation: The correct Law of Cosines formula is c² = a² + b² - 2ab·cos(C).

quiz.q: When angle C = 90°, the Law of Cosines reduces to:
quiz.explanation: When C = 90°, cos(90°) = 0, so c² = a² + b² - 0 = a² + b² (the Pythagorean theorem).

quiz.q: Heron's formula requires knowing:
quiz.explanation: Heron’s formula computes area from three sides: Area = √(s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)) where s = (a+b+c)/2.

quiz.q: The semiperimeter of a triangle with sides 3, 4, 5 is:

lessons.title: Inverse Trigonometric Functions
lessons.description: Understand and evaluate inverse sine, cosine, and tangent functions.
lessons.formula:
Inverse Trigonometric Functions:

y = sin⁻¹(x) means sin(y) = x
  Domain: [-1, 1], Range: [-π/2, π/2]

y = cos⁻¹(x) means cos(y) = x
  Domain: [-1, 1], Range: [0, π]

y = tan⁻¹(x) means tan(y) = x
  Domain: (-∞, ∞), Range: (-π/2, π/2)
lessons.content:
Regular trigonometric functions take an angle and produce a ratio, but inverse trigonometric functions do the opposite: they take a ratio and produce an angle. The inverse sine (also called arcsine), written sin⁻¹(x), answers the question “what angle has a sine value of x?” However, since trigonometric functions are not one-to-one (they repeat values), we must restrict their domains to create proper inverse functions that pass the horizontal line test.

The restricted ranges are carefully chosen to give unique outputs: sin⁻¹(x) has range [-π/2, π/2] (Quadrants I and IV), cos⁻¹(x) has range [0, π] (Quadrants I and II), and tan⁻±(x) has range (-π/2, π/2) (Quadrants I and IV). These ranges are known as the principal values. It is crucial to remember that sin⁻¹(x) always returns an angle in [-π/2, π/2]—it will never return an angle in Quadrant II or III, even if there are valid angles there with the same sine value.

The domains of the inverse trig functions are also restricted: sin⁻¹(x) and cos⁻¹(x) only accept inputs between -1 and 1 (since sine and cosine outputs are bounded), while tan⁻¹(x) accepts any real number. Attempting to evaluate sin⁻¹(2) is undefined since no angle has a sine value of 2. Compositions of inverse and regular trig functions follow specific rules: sin(sin⁻¹(x)) = x for x in [-1, 1], but sin⁻¹(sin(x)) only equals x when x is in the restricted range [-π/2, π/2].
steps: Identify the inverse function needed and verify the input is within the domain ([-1, 1] for sin⁻¹/cos⁻¹, all reals for tan⁻¹).
Determine the output range: sin⁻± returns [-π/2, π/2], cos⁻± returns [0, π], tan⁻± returns (-π/2, π/2).
Evaluate using the unit circle: find the angle in the correct range whose trig value equals the input.
For compositions: sin(sin⁻±(x)) = x (always), but sin⁻±(sin(x)) = x only if x is in the restricted range.
For expressions like cos(sin⁻±(x)), draw a right triangle: let θ = sin⁻±(x), then find cos(θ) using Pythagorean relationships.

examples.title: Evaluate sin⁻¹(1/2)
examples.text: sin⁻¹(1/2) asks: which angle in [-π/2, π/2] has sin = 1/2? From the unit circle, sin(π/6) = 1/2, and π/6 is in the correct range. So sin⁻¹(1/2) = π/6.

examples.title: Evaluate cos(sin⁻±(3/5))
examples.text: Let θ = sin⁻¹(3/5), so sin(θ) = 3/5. Draw a right triangle: opposite = 3, hypotenuse = 5. Adjacent = √(25-9) = 4. So cos(θ) = 4/5, meaning cos(sin⁻¹(3/5)) = 4/5.

lessons.tip: Memorize the restricted ranges! sin⁻±: [-π/2, π/2], cos⁻±: [0, π], tan⁻±: (-π/2, π/2). For cos⁻±, the range is Quadrants I and II only. This is the most tested concept on inverse trig questions.

quiz.q: What is cos⁻¹(-1)?
quiz.explanation: cos⁻¹(-1) asks: which angle in [0, π] has cos = -1? cos(π) = -1, so the answer is π.

quiz.q: The range of sin⁻¹(x) is:
quiz.explanation: The range of arcsine is restricted to [-π/2, π/2], which covers Quadrants I and IV.

quiz.q: tan⁻¹(1) = π/4. What is tan⁻¹(-1)?
quiz.explanation: tan(-π/4) = -1, and -π/4 is in the range (-π/2, π/2). So tan⁻¹(-1) = -π/4.

quiz.q: Which expression is undefined?
quiz.explanation: sin⁻¹(2) is undefined because the domain of sin⁻¹ is [-1, 1], and 2 is outside this range.

lessons.title: Applications: Navigation and Surveying
lessons.description: Apply trigonometry to real-world problems including navigation, surveying, and engineering.
lessons.formula:
Angle of Elevation:
tan(θ) = height/distance
height = distance × tan(θ)
distance = height/tan(θ)

Angle of Depression = Angle of Elevation
(alternate interior angles)

Navigation Bearings:
Bearing measured clockwise from north
Bearing 045° = 45° east of north
Bearing 270° = due west
lessons.content:
Trigonometry is indispensable in the real world, and one of its most practical applications is in navigation and surveying. The angle of elevation is the angle between the horizontal line of sight and the line looking upward to an object. The angle of depression is the angle between the horizontal and the line looking downward. A key fact: the angle of elevation from point A to point B equals the angle of depression from point B to point A, because they are alternate interior angles formed by parallel horizontal lines.

In surveying, a common problem is finding the height of an inaccessible object like a building, cliff, or tree. The surveyor measures the angle of elevation from a known distance away and uses the tangent ratio: height = distance × tan(angle). For very tall objects, the surveyor may take two measurements from different positions and use the Law of Sines to eliminate the need to measure the distance to the base directly. This technique is called triangulation and is the basis for GPS positioning systems.

In navigation, bearings describe direction as an angle measured clockwise from due north. A bearing of 045° means 45° east of north (northeast), while 315° means 45° west of north (northwest). Pilots and sailors use bearings constantly, and solving navigation problems requires converting between bearings and standard position angles, then applying the Law of Sines or Law of Cosines to find distances and headings. Engineers use these same principles to design roads, determine sight distances for safe driving, and calculate the heights of cell towers and bridges.
steps: Draw a diagram of the situation, labeling all known distances, angles, and unknown quantities.
Identify right triangles in the diagram and label the angle of elevation or depression.
Choose the appropriate trigonometric ratio (usually tangent for height/distance problems).
Set up the equation using the known values and solve for the unknown.
For navigation problems, convert bearings to standard angles, then apply the Law of Sines or Cosines as needed.

examples.title: Finding the Height of a Building
examples.text: From a point 50 feet from the base of a building, the angle of elevation to the top is 35°. Using tan(35°) = height/50: height = 50 × tan(35°) = 50 × 0.7002 ≈ 35.0 feet.

examples.title: Ship Navigation Problem
examples.text: A ship sails on a bearing of 060° for 15 miles, then turns to a bearing of 150° for 10 miles. The angle between the two legs is 90°. Using Pythagorean theorem: distance back to start = √(15² + 10²) = √325 ≈ 18.03 miles.

lessons.tip: Always draw a picture for word problems! Label the horizontal line, mark the angle of elevation or depression, and identify which sides you know and which you need. The diagram makes the trig ratio choice obvious.

quiz.q: The angle of elevation from the ground to the top of a 100m tower is 45°. How far is the observer from the tower?
quiz.explanation: tan(45°) = 100/distance, so distance = 100/tan(45°) = 100/1 = 100m.

quiz.q: A bearing of 270° means the direction is:
quiz.explanation: Bearings are measured clockwise from north. 270° clockwise from north = due west.

quiz.q: The angle of depression from a lighthouse to a boat equals the angle of elevation from the boat to the lighthouse because:
quiz.explanation: Horizontal lines are parallel, making the angles of elevation and depression alternate interior angles, which are equal.

quiz.q: A surveyor measures an angle of elevation of 30° from 200 feet away. The height is:
